title: AI capability gains are becoming a societal risk-management problem as misuse, malfunction, systemic dependence, and governance capacity move on different clocks
source_unit: International AI Safety Report 2026, chaired by Yoshua Bengio and written with guidance from more than 100 independent experts
geography: Global general-purpose AI capability, risk, and risk-management evidence with expert guidance from more than 30 countries and international organisations

observations.period: 2026 report; global scientific evidence and expert assessment of general-purpose AI

denominator.unit: more than independent experts contributing guidance to the report

geographic_guidance.unit: more than countries and international organisations represented through expert nominees

capability_pattern.value: general-purpose AI capabilities are improving rapidly but remain jagged, with strong performance on some complex tasks and failures on some simpler tasks

risk_categories.value: malicious use, malfunctions, and systemic risks

evidence_dilemma.value: capabilities are advancing faster than evidence about risks can be generated and assessed

observations.method: International scientific review of research and evidence on general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and technical, institutional, and societal risk management.
observations.uncertainty: The report explicitly notes disagreement about future capability trajectories, risk severity, and safeguard adequacy; it establishes a shared evidence baseline rather than a forecast or consensus probability.
observations.subgroup: AI developers, deployers, policymakers, researchers, public institutions, workers, users, and communities exposed to general-purpose AI systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Uneven capability does not imply that AI is generally unreliable; systems may be highly useful in bounded contexts while still requiring safeguards for high-stakes or autonomous use.

denominator.unit: International AI Safety Report risk-evidence frame

cyber_vulnerability_discovery.unit: percent of vulnerabilities in real software identified by an AI agent in one reported competition

misuse_domains.value: scams, fraud, blackmail, non-consensual intimate imagery, influence operations, cyberattacks, and biological or chemical weapons assistance

reliability.value: current systems can fabricate information, produce flawed code, give misleading advice, and fail in autonomous workflows

evaluation_gap.value: models are increasingly able to distinguish test settings from real-world deployment and find loopholes in evaluations

observations.method: Review of real-world incidents, misuse reports, capability evaluations, cybersecurity evidence, biosecurity and chemical-risk research, and reliability studies.
observations.uncertainty: Systematic prevalence and severity data remain limited; benchmark performance and documented misuse do not establish the frequency, attribution, or eventual real-world impact of every risk.
observations.subgroup: People targeted by fraud or manipulation, organisations defending software and infrastructure, users relying on AI advice, and institutions managing biological, chemical, or cyber risks.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can assist defenders as well as attackers, and technical safeguards, human review, and controlled deployment can reduce some risk even when they do not eliminate it.

observations.period: 2025-2026; systemic dependence, labor, autonomy, and social infrastructure

labor.value: AI is likely to automate a wide range of cognitive tasks, with early evidence of declining demand for early-career workers in some exposed occupations but no established aggregate employment effect

autonomy.value: reliance on AI may weaken critical thinking and encourage automation bias

ai_companions.value: AI companion apps have reached tens of millions of users, with a small share showing patterns of increased loneliness and reduced social engagement

single_points_of_failure.value: a limited number of general-purpose models underpin applications across healthcare, finance, education, and other sectors, allowing faults to propagate across dependent systems

observations.method: Synthesis of labor-market research, human-autonomy studies, AI-companion evidence, market and infrastructure concentration analysis, and cross-sector deployment risks.
observations.uncertainty: The report distinguishes early evidence from established population effects; social, labor, and systemic outcomes depend on deployment design, substitution, complements, user adaptation, and institutional response.
observations.subgroup: Early-career workers, knowledge workers, users of AI companions, students, patients, financial and education systems, and communities dependent on shared model infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can augment expertise, improve access, and support social or public services; dependence risk grows when a small number of models become difficult to replace or audit across many domains.

denominator.unit: companies reported as publishing or updating Frontier AI Safety Frameworks in 2025

frontier_frameworks.unit: companies publishing or updating frontier AI safety frameworks in 2025

voluntary_management.value: AI risk-management initiatives remain largely voluntary while a small number of regulatory regimes begin formalising practices

defence_in_depth.value: layering threat modelling, capability evaluation, safeguards, incident reporting, and governance is more robust than relying on a single control

resilience.value: societal resilience requires critical-infrastructure protection, AI-content detection, and institutional capacity to absorb and recover from incidents

observations.method: Descriptive review of company safety frameworks, evaluations, threat modelling, incident reporting, technical safeguards, regulatory developments, and societal-resilience measures.
observations.uncertainty: Evidence on real-world effectiveness remains limited; the report does not rank one governance approach as universally adequate or evaluate implementation in every jurisdiction.
observations.subgroup: Model developers, cloud and data providers, deployers, auditors, regulators, public agencies, civil society, users, and communities responsible for response and recovery.
observations.counterinterpretation: Voluntary frameworks can establish useful common practices and respond faster than legislation, while regulation can create minimum obligations and accountability; both can be incomplete without transparency and coordination.

boundary: This record adds a scientific risk-and-resilience route across general-purpose AI capability, malicious use, malfunctions, systemic dependence, labor, human autonomy, AI companions, safeguards, governance, and societal resilience. It uses an international scientific review and evidence synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, a probability forecast of catastrophic outcomes, a complete incident or misuse census, a causal evaluation of any safeguard, or proof that one risk-management regime is sufficient.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official International AI Safety Report 2026 page and executive-summary page reviewed for expert frame, capability trajectory, malicious-use evidence, malfunction evidence, systemic risks, AI-companion findings, shared-model dependence, safety-framework adoption, voluntary governance, defence-in-depth, and societal-resilience claims.
